newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Credit Suisse, Winterthur to merge.
newsitem.headline: Credit Suisse, Winterthur to merge.

text.p: Two of Switzerland's top financial groups, Credit Suisse Group and Winterthur Group, Monday announced plans to merge and create one of the world's leading financial service providers.

The deal catapults Credit Suisse Group into the position of undisputed leader among Switzerland's Big Three banks, taking place amid deep structural changes in global financial markets and fierce competition in the insurance industry.
"The merger is a powerful, forward-looking response to developments in the financial services market," said Lukas Muehlemann, chief executive of the combined group.

The stock market reacted positively to the announcement and industry analysts were also in favour of the move, noting it is likely to put pressure on Union Bank of Switzerland UBS and Swiss Bank Corp. SBC to meet the challenge.
"I think this puts pressure on the other big Swiss banks," said Thomas Della Putta of private bankers Pictet & Cie.

The merger comes after months of intense speculation about Winterthur and only days after financier Martin Ebner said he wanted to acquire a majority of the insurer. One analyst questioned whether the timing of the merger was dictated by the stake amassed in Winterthur by Ebner's BZ Group.

The combination of Credit Suisse, currently Switzerland's second-largest bank, with Winterthur, the third-largest insurer, should result in gains of 300 million to 350 million Swiss francs ($199 million to $232 million) within three years from higher income and cost-cutting.
A maximum of 500 jobs worldwide will be lost due to attrition, but the companies said in a joint statement that there would be no layoffs.

"The two companies are now in an even better position to provide their personal and corporate customers with attractive financial products combining the advantages of banking and insurance solutions," the companies said.

Shareholders of both companies will be asked to approve the deal on Sept. 5. Assuming approval, Credit Suisse Group will offer Winterthur shareholders to swap one of their shares for 7.3 Credit Suisse shares.

Winterthur will then become part of the Credit Suisse Group, boosting its total assets to around 700 billion francs ($463 billion), giving it a market capitalisation of more than 50 billion ($33 billion) and around 700 billion francs ($463 billion) in assets under management.
The merger illustrates the blurring distinction between banks and insurance companies, where market position and market presence is becoming increasingly critical.

"Strategically, this makes sense for Credit Suisse. The general trend in Europe clearly goes toward bancassurance. It's not the insurance companies that need the banks, it's the banks that need the insurance companies to be more competitive," said Della Putta.
"The merger will allow the group to exploit to the full the advantages of being a banassurance provider in all customer and market segments," the companies said.

Credit Suisse Group, reporting its half-year results early due to the merger announcement, said preliminary figures showed net profit surged 70 percent to around 1.41 billion Swiss francs ($933 million) in the first half of 1997.
Net profit growth was at the high end of growth estimates, which had run between 45 and 90 percent.
